extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students studying infringement doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-treatise guidance on doctrines and standards used to determine patent infringement (machines, processes, compositions, designs), with cases and examples illustrating when changes, equivalents, later patents, and utility affect infringement. Focused on U.S. patent law principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal construction for inventions of exceptional merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though an invention is not generic, if it is one of exceptional merit it is entitled to a liberal construction and a fair range of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patented invention is especially meritorious, courts may construe its claims broadly and allow a wider range of equivalents than for ordinary patents. (Cited in text as a recognized rule.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidential weight of a later patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant of a subsequent patent is frequently said to raise a legal presumption of patentable difference from an earlier invention, but that presumption is limited and does not itself establish non-infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between improvements over prior structures and inventions of a different species. A later patent may embody things that are exclusive to the earlier patentee; Patent Office findings of patentable difference concern disclosure, not claim scope. The later patent is not evidence of non-infringement unless the earlier patent is shown to be specific (narrow) so that the later patent's claims neither improve nor embody the earlier claims. Cases (e.g., Kokomo, Herman v. Youngstown) illustrate limits and exceptions. The Commissioner’s interference determination may overcome or affect the presumption in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent grants only exclusionary right (not a right to make/use)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is not the grant of a right to make or use or sell; it grants only the right to exclude others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a patent is only the right to exclude, the mere issuance of a later patent does not create a right to practice an earlier patent's subject-matter and therefore does not automatically negate infringement. This principle undercuts arguments that a subsequent patent necessarily defeats infringement claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of form generally does not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A change of form does not avoid an infringement of a patent unless the form shown in the patent is necessary to the functions ascribed to the invention, is the distinguishing characteristic of the invention, is essential to its patentability, or the patentee specifies a particular form as the means of producing the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even changes that modify construction, action, or utility seldom avoid infringement. Examples include curved guides replaced by broken lines (Ives v. Hamilton), pavement block shape changes, and rock-boring head modifications. Courts collect instances to show that mere changes in form are immaterial unless one of the listed exceptions applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structures made to evade the spirit but containing claimed elements infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures designed merely for the purpose of evading the spirit of the invention but which contain all the elements of the claims are infringements of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding an easily discarded part that may or may not be used by the purchaser will not avoid infringement if the accused device contains all claimed elements. Attempts to evade by artifice fail where the normal/easiest/effective use would infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal/useful mode of use controls infringement analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing that the accused structure may occasionally be used in a manner that would not infringe does not avert infringement if the structure, when used in the normal, easiest, and most effective way, infringes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look at how the device is normally used; sporadic non-infringing uses are insufficient to defeat infringement where the ordinary use falls within the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of composition patents depends on sameness/equivalence and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement of patents for compositions of matter depends upon sameness or equivalence of ingredients and upon substantial sameness of the proportions of those ingredients; omission of an ingredient avoids infringement; addition that substantially changes character avoids infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like mechanical combinations, omission of a claimed ingredient defeats infringement. Additions that materially alter character avoid infringement; trivial or insubstantial additions made to evade liability will not avoid infringement. Determination often requires chemical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertainment of composition is technical and limited to proper tests
rubrics_metrics.description: The ascertainment of the character of a composition of matter is work for chemists and consists in the application of proper tests to each case; a patentee is confined to proper tests of identity and cannot impose an improper test by stating it in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants may invoke all proper tests of identity specified or not in the patent; patentees cannot require courts to accept improper analytical tests merely because the patent mentions them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of equivalents in compositions generally does not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution of one equivalent for another in a patented composition of matter is generally as ineffectual to avoid infringement as like substitution in a machine; an equivalent is anything which in that composition performs the same function as the ingredient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal equivalency is determined by function, not necessarily by chemical identity. Examples include mica powder found equivalent to infusorial earth in dynamite despite differing behavior; chemical classification alone does not determine legal equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical equivalency not necessary for legal equivalency
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical equivalency is not necessary to legal equivalency between substances in respect of a non-chemical use of those substances; the term 'equivalent' means 'equally good' regarding ingredients of compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute ingredients that perform the same function (even if they also perform additional functions) can be equivalents. Classification by chemists or common groupings does not automatically make substances legal equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on monopolizing a claimed group via doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent states that each member of a group of substances can be used and some members cannot be so used, the patentee cannot later invoke the doctrine of equivalents to monopolize all members subsequently found suitable; a generic claim purporting to cover matter from any prescribed starting material is void if some members are unsuitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific claim limited to a particular suitable starting material may still be valid even if a generic claim in the same patent is not. The doctrine prevents patentees from claiming by equivalence what they expressly admitted was unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee can disclaim particular equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent expressly states that the composition does not include a specified ingredient or otherwise disclaims a particular equivalent, substitution of that ingredient avoids infringement and the disclaimer is binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee's explicit disclaimers of equivalents are enforceable even if unnecessary; they restrict the patentee’s later claim to exclude that equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in proportions: small changes vs operative changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes of the proportions of the ingredients of a composition will not avoid infringement where those changes do not affect its essential character; but changes that change the operative character, together with changes in mode of manufacture, may avert infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor variations that only alter bulk or cost typically do not avoid infringement; courts will examine whether proportion changes materially alter the composition's operative function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent infringement judged by ordinary observers (appearance test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent is infringed by any design which, to general observers interested in the subject or to purchasers of similar things, has the same appearance as that of the patented design; designs are to be judged by synthetic observation rather than analytic inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare two articles as they appear in use; the test is sameness of aesthetic effect on the eye, not whether an ordinary purchaser might be deceived. Experts' analytic opinions are less important than average observers' impressions. Design patents cover appearance only, not uses; use in a non-analogous manner can still be infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative utility alone is not determinative of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparative utility of the plaintiff's and the defendant's process, machine, manufacture, or composition is not alone a criterion of infringement; constructing the patented thing imperfectly to diminish utility does not avoid infringement, nor does a defendant's superior machine that is nevertheless an addition to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a defendant's superiority results from an addition to the patented combination, that superiority does not avoid infringement even if the addition is patentable. However, if the defendant discovered an entirely different mode of construction/operation (a different species), it may avoid infringement. Comparative utility is relevant only when coupled with comparative character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species vs genus: different species do not infringe each other
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's machine may be of a different species and thus cannot infringe a patent of a different species, though both might infringe a genus patent of which they are species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether accused device and claimed invention are same species or merely species of a common genus; species-level differences can defeat infringement even if genus claims might read on both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge or intent of infringer is irrelevant to liability
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute an infringement it is not necessary that the infringer should have known of the patent's existence or that his doings constituted an infringement; independent invention does not avert liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement is a strict-liability rule regarding unauthorized making/using/selling of claimed subject matter. Cases cited show lack of notice or independent conception are not defenses.
